text:
One famous 1967 study by Ramirez & Luza found it more effective than the best antipsychotic drugs at the time, slashing mental patients' psych ward stays in half, although it hasn't been tested (that I know of, yet) specifically for anxiety or PTSD, although those patients surely had both of those conditions. It's routinely used in humans who receive stem cell transplants, as it is the best cell preservative that we've found so far. There is evidence (Kortleve, et al, 2023) that using too much DMSO (10% vs 5%) in stem cell transfusions increases mild side effects in adult humans.

DMSO also appears to kill brain cells when they're exposed to it for too long, as it did in baby mice (from birth to 30 days old) and in a dish of rat neurons (Hanslick, et al, 2009). Translating mouse research to humans isn't straightforward.
section: DMSO (Mental Stabilizers That Don't Abort the Trip)
reader: someone reading the guide's DMSO profile, before or between trips, deciding whether and how to use DMSO to steady a bad trip, weighing what the research says it does and its risks

sentences.payoff: they know the risk to brain cells is in long exposure and in young brains, so they keep it short
sentences.follows: a second downside, to brain cells
sentences.link: DMSO also appears to kill brain cells

sentences.payoff: they weigh the mouse finding as uncertain for people
sentences.follows: it weighs the finding before it

checked.found: DMSO caused widespread apoptosis in the developing brains of mice from birth to 30 days old, worst at 7 days, from 0.3 ml/kg, and neuron loss in rat hippocampal cultures at 0.5% and 1.0% (the abstract, read 2026-11-13; his "healthy mice neurons" said as what it found, which he said yes to at 14:56 UTC)
checked.still_needed: yes: they keep the exposure short, and know young brains were the ones harmed

question_text.Q1: Why am I reading this sentence, and do I know it before I have to work through it? (the point first, in each sentence and each paragraph; a study after the question it answers; a term explained where it is first used, never in a sentence after it)
question_text.Q2: What is each instruction for, said in the reader's terms, and is it something the helper does ("have someone go with them"), not a rule stated as a fact ("someone goes with them")?
question_text.Q3: Which thing exactly? (pools of water, not water; any substance, not anything)
question_text.Q4: What does each word act on, or mean here? (adjunct remedy; known-genuine) Is every term a high-school graduate wouldn't know (enterocytes, BPC-157) explained once, where it is first used, and common ones (a vitamin) left alone? Is each mechanism explained by what it does in the reader's experience (dopamine "for motivation (by showing us what is important to pay attention to)"; DeltaFosB "preventing that learning from really clicking"), not by where it sits or what it looks like ("a chemical blanket", "the slower one underneath")? (E375)
question_text.Q5: Why does each sentence follow from the one before? (every but, so, because and this has what it turns on)
question_text.Q6: Is this the order the reader is thinking in, and does each idea sit next to what it continues?
question_text.Q7: Does each fact help this reader now, in their case (the same kind of thing they face, not just the same topic)?
question_text.Q8: Does each item belong in the group it is put in?
